title: Hydrothermal fluids from the Eastern Himalaya Syntaxis and Tengchong Volcanic Field, southeast Tibet: Geochemical constraints on deep-sourced carbon contributions
description: Publication date: Available online 27 May 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry Author(s): Jujing Li, Zhengfu Guo, Wenbin Zhao, Xiangang Xie, Yutao Sun, Guichun He
abstract: Volcanoes and large-scale strike-slip faults constitute primary conduits for transporting deep-sourced fluids, including carbon, to the Earth’s surface. However, comparative studies that link geothermal anomalies with deep carbon fluxes, as well as the mechanisms governing regional fluid circulation, remain scarce. Here we present a systematic hydrogeochemical investigation of thermal springs from the Eastern Himalayan Syntaxis (EHS) and the Tengchong Volcanic Field (TVF) in southeastern Tibet, integrating major ion compositions, stable isotopes (δD, δ18O), and dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC) isotopes. Our results show that TVF springs are predominantly of Na–HCO3 and Na–Cl types, whereas EHS springs exhibit Na–HCO3, Na–Cl, and Ca–HCO3 types. Rehai (TVF) springs of the SO4 type suggest a magmatic heat effect. Based on oxygen and hydrogen isotope data, recharge elevations range from 4182 to 5397 m for the EHS and from 1530 to 2637 m for the TVF. Geothermometry reveals distinct circulation depths: 2205–5464 m in the EHS core zone, decreasing to 978–1861 m in the west. Qualitative water-rock interaction analysis supports a dominant role of deep-sourced carbon. By combining our DIC data with previously published gas CO2 compositions from the same springs, we quantitatively estimate that deep-sourced carbon (mantle- and metamorphic-derived CO2) contributes 57.5–93.9% of the spring DIC pool in both regions. Our findings offer new constraints on the contribution of continental collision zones to endogenic CO2 fluxes and their potential implications for long-term climate evolution.

title: Mapping the distribution and historical preservation of lipophilic marine algal toxins in sediments of the Bohai and Northern Yellow seas
description: Publication date: Available online 27 May 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry Author(s): Haoshun Zhang, Xiuping He, Tongzhu Han, Xiaofei Yin, Junhui Chen
abstract: The marine benthic environment provides habitat for many fishery organisms. Lipophilic marine algal toxins (LMATs) can accumulate in coastal sediments, where they pose risks to benthic ecosystems and fishery organisms through trophic transfer. However, understanding of the distribution and burial patterns of LMATs in coastal sediments remains limited. Here, LMATs in surface sediments, porewater, and box sediment cores from the Bohai Sea and the northern Yellow Sea of China were systematically investigated. The composition, phase partitioning, spatial distribution, and vertical distribution of LMATs were characterized, and the suitability of sedimentary LMATs as biomarkers was assessed. Thirteen LMATs were detected in the sedimentary environment, including pectenotoxin–2 (PTX2), okadaic acid (OA), azaspiracid–1 (AZA1), azaspiracid–2 (AZA2), gymnodimine (GYM), yessotoxin (YTX), hydroxy–yessotoxin (h–YTX), two PTX2 homologs, and four PTX2 isomers, with the PTX2 isomers reported for the first time in marine sediments. In surface sediments from the Bohai Sea and the northern Yellow Sea, PTX2 (including isomers) was the dominant LMAT, accounting for an average of 56.88%, followed by YTX and h–YTX. PTX2 and OA were the principal LMATs in porewater and exhibited different partitioning behaviors at the sediment–porewater interface. ∑LMAT concentrations in sediments of the northern Yellow Sea (mean 248.5 ng/kg) were significantly higher than those in the Bohai Sea (mean 98.3 ng/kg), with elevated values near the coastal areas of Qinhuangdao (Hebei Province) and Weihai (Shandong Province). ∑LMAT concentrations generally decreased with increasing depth in sediment cores. OA, YTX, and h–YTX were restricted to upper core sections, whereas PTX2 and AZA2 occurred throughout the cores and showed localized concentration maxima at specific depths. Overall, PTX2 and AZA2 exhibit strong stability in deep sediments and show potential as biomarkers for reconstructing the historical occurrence of marine toxigenic algae.

title: Multi-parameter soil gas geochemistry and fracture-controlled degassing along the İzmir Fault (Western Türkiye)
description: Publication date: Available online 27 May 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry Author(s): Mutlu İçhedef, Caner Taşköprü, İlayda Sapmaz, Fulsen Özen, Gözde Duman, Emre Tabar, Hasan Sözbilir, Salvatore Giammanco
abstract: In this study, soil gas concentrations of 222Rn (Radon), 220Rn (Thoron), and CO2 were measured along the İzmir Fault Zone in western Türkiye to investigate the relationship between gas anomalies and fault-controlled permeability. A total of 342 measurement points were systematically sampled along the two segments of the İzmir Fault (IF), spatial variations of soil gas concentrations were analyzed to identify locations that indicate anomalies. 222Rn (Radon), 220Rn (Thoron), and CO2 concentrations were determined in soil gas in the areas surrounding the fault. Quantile–quantile (Q–Q) plots were used to determine anomaly thresholds for each parameter, and concentration values exceeding these thresholds were classified as anomalies. The results reveal significant spatial variability in soil gas concentrations along the fault system. Although anomalies were detected in both segments of the İzmir Fault, multiple gas anomalies were predominantly concentrated at the westernmost end of the Balçova–Narlıdere segment. This result suggests the following regarding fault activity: The concentration of multi-gas anomalies along the Balçova–Narlıdere segment suggests active degassing processes along this part of the fault. This pattern suggests that gas distribution in the study area is not solely controlled by distance to the main fault line, but may instead reflect the heterogeneous permeability structure of the fault zone and the influence of localized fractures and preferential migration pathways. These findings demonstrate that integrated soil gas measurements provide an effective geochemical approach for identifying structurally controlled gas migration pathways and localized degassing zones in active tectonic environments.

title: Mineral phase transformation drives molecular fractionation of dissolved organic matter during organic acid-driven weathering of bauxite residue
description: Publication date: 20 September 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 719 Author(s): Chenglong Lu, Songlin Wu, Fang You, Dingyi Yu, Jitraporn Vongsvivut, Annaleise Klein, Lars Thomsen, David Parry, Ting-Shan Chan, Longbin Huang
abstract: Dissolved organic matter (DOM) sequestration is critical to soil formation of bauxite residue (BR) in which BR undergoes mineral weathering and neutralization / acidification driven by microbial and/or plant root-derived organic acids (OA). The present study aimed to understand the molecular fractionation and adsorption of DOM in BR minerals during key stages of mineral weathering and neutralization, using mixed organic acids to simulate the mineral weathering process in the ecological engineering context. Selective adsorption and molecular fractionation of DOM derived from microbial decomposition of plant mulch were characterized using the high-resolution electrospray ionization Orbitrap mass spectrometry (Orbitrap-MS). The OA-treatments progressively weathered sodalite-like alkaline minerals to form amorphous Al/Si/Fe phases and lowered pH, increasing surface reactive sites in mineral phases. The slightly weathered (pH 9–7) and highly weathered and acidified BR minerals (pH 5–4), preferentially adsorbed high-molecular-weight organics rich in aromatic and/or polyphenolic domains. Synchrotron-based Al, Si, and Fe K-edge X ray absorption spectroscopic analyses (XAS) and Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) mapping, revealed strong associations of secondary Al/Si/Fe phases with protein-, carboxylic-, aromatic-, and oxygenated lipid-like compounds. These findings highlight the critical role of mineral weathering in BR for controlling the stabilization of DOM during eco-engineered soil formation processes.

title: Geochemistry of Amazonian ironstone microbialites and their significance as paleoenvironmental archives
description: Publication date: 5 September 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 718 Author(s): Marília Prado Freire, Cécile Gautheron, Stéphane Guédron, Bastien Wild, Sylvain Campillo, Sabine Sentenac, Rachel Martin, Valérie Magnin, André Oliveira Sawakuchi, Cristiano Mazur Chiessi, Dailson A. Bertassoli, Ana Maria Goes
abstract: New type of paleoclimatic and paleoenvironmental archives are critically needed in tropical continental areas to better reconstruct multimillennial to multimillion year climate and environmental changes, as classical archives such as speleothems or well-preserved sediments are frequently not available because they are poorly preserved. We examined Pleistocene continental ironstones that are laminated ferruginous crusts formed by the lithification of ferruginous microbialites made of goethite that entrapped coarse to fine siliciclastic grains at different scales (micrometer to few centimeters). Samples were collected from ironstones, formed and exposed in the rapids of the Xingu River, eastern Amazonia (Brazil). Major, trace, and rare earth elements (REE) composition from the microscale to the mesoscale were analyzed in different ironstone samples together with bacterial and fungal diversity to examine their potential as paleoclimatic and/or paleoenvironmental archives. Results indicate that ferruginous ironstones, are composed of finely laminated goethite that conserve their geochemistry after fossilization and have not been affected by secondary diagenetic processes. Changes in Al and P composition in particles entrapped within the goethite lamina and the whole samples are associated with enrichment in redox sensitive elements (e.g., As, V), which can be attributed to periods of lower river hydrological regime. In contrast, coarser and heterolithic ironstone, i.e., ferruginous sandstone trapping quartz grains, with aluminosilicates and psilomelane (MnBa rich mineral) rich in metals (e.g., Pb, Hg, REE) and refractory elements (e.g., Ti, Rb, Zr) were attributed to wetter epochs and higher river water regime. Secondary psilomelane phases are also observed in fracture showing a late precipitation after the ironstone fossilization. From published dating of a decimetric laminated ironstone layer, it is estimated that each laminae recorded information at the decadal to secular scale. The combination of micrometric to mesoscopic geochemical data supports that high resolution studies of Xingu laminated ironstones will provide major insights into paleoclimatic and paleoenvironmental changes in the Amazon basin by focusing on both lithotypes of the ironstones.

title: Distribution and migration pattern of lithium in two tonsteins inside the Li-rich coal under groundwater and seawater leaching
description: Publication date: 5 September 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 718 Author(s): Huidi Hao, Bo Jiu, Wenhui Huang, Zhenguang Shang, Zhaoguo Wang, Li Long, Linghao Huang, Yingying Zhao, Haonan Chen
abstract: The migration and enrichment mechanisms of lithium (Li) in coal-hosted tonsteins under groundwater and seawater leaching are poorly understood. This study investigates two tonstein samples from the Late Carboniferous No. 6 coal seam in the Jungar Coalfield, Ordos Basin, China, using an integrated approach that combines mineralogical, bulk-geochemical, and in-situ microanalytical techniques (TIMA, SEM-EDS, LA-ICP-MS) to elucidate the role of fluid-rock interactions in Li redistribution. The Li in the upper tonstein was primarily influenced by groundwater and occurs as lattice-bound Li within vermicular kaolinite, which replaced Al3+ through isomorphic substitution (Al3+ + Li+ → Si4+). Furthermore, the Li content in this unit exhibits a distinct trend of increasing in coarser crystals. In contrast, Li in the lower seawater-leached tonstein was initially scavenged via surface complexation onto the high-surface-area cryptocrystalline kaolinite and subsequently stabilized. Fluid composition exerts a key control: while the primary Li source was the volcanic precursors, seawater infiltration, indicated by high Sr/Ba ratios, elevated boron contents, and Mg/Sr signatures in the fracture-filling calcite, significantly enhanced Li mobilization and its subsequent adsorption onto clay surfaces, whereas groundwater of terrestrial origin showed limited mobilization and transport efficiency. Furthermore, the systematic decrease in Li concentrations away from calcite-filled fractures confirms their role as primary conduits for seawater infiltration, while coal permeability and the organic matrix governed the spatial heterogeneity of enrichment. This study characterizes the mechanisms of Li accumulation in tonsteins by comparing the contrasting roles of seawater and meteoric groundwater. Our findings demonstrate that seawater leaching of volcanic precursors is a significantly more effective driver for Li super-enrichment than meteoric groundwater leaching, thereby providing a more precise framework for assessing the potential of Li resources in coal-bearing sequences.

title: From serpentinization to carbonation: Petrological and geochemical constraints from an ophiolitic reaction profile
description: Publication date: Available online 26 May 2026 Source: Chemical Geology Author(s): Hong-Da Zheng, Qing Xiong, Xiang Zhou, Biao Chang, Hong-Kun Dai, Hong-Zhu Cai, Li Wang, Yi-Cong Li, Long-Fei Xue, Ming Chen, Jian-Ping Zheng
abstract: Peridotite carbonation, commonly along with serpentinization, is efficient for carbon sequestration in Earth's carbon cycle. However, the interplay of the two processes and the fluid-rock reactions remain elusive. Here we present a ~ 330-m-long fluid-peridotite reaction profile with a southward zonation of harzburgite, serpentinite to soapstone-bearing listvenite in the Luobusa ophiolite (Tibet). The systematic variations of volatile-free whole-rock major-element compositions and consistent trace-element patterns suggest variable peridotitic protoliths. From harzburgite to listvenite, H2O+ contents firstly increase and then abruptly drop once the carbonation initiates as evidenced by a jump in CO2 contents, suggesting progressive serpentinization to carbonation. The Fe3+/FeT ratios elevate during the progress of serpentinization, and then decrease after the onset of carbonation. These variations indicate that the serpentinization and carbonation involved distinct redox processes, causing strong variations in H2 fugacity in the reaction system and controlling the compositional variations of involved fluids and the crystallization of zoned magnesites. Clumped isotopes constrain the carbonation temperatures up to ~192–302 °C. C-O isotopic compositions suggest that the fluids were derived primarily from wall-rock meta-graywackes. In addition, thermodynamic modelling shows that the mineralogical, chemical and redox variations from serpentinization to carbonation are consistent with those observed in the Luobusa profile. Such CO2-rich fluids migrated along the trans-lithospheric thrust in Himalaya and reacted with the Luobusa ophiolite. This study shows that natural serpentinization and carbonation may have limited capacity for carbon sequestration, and complete carbonation of ultramafic massifs requires external forces to produce new fractures for fluid-peridotite reactions.

title: Optimizing acid digestion protocols for osmium isotope analysis of Quaternary marine sediments
description: Publication date: Available online 25 May 2026 Source: Chemical Geology Author(s): G.A. Goss, A.D. Rooney
abstract: The marine osmium (Os) isotope system has become a powerful proxy for reconstructing Quaternary Earth surface processes, owing to its favorable geochemical properties and advances in analytical precision. However, variations in acid digestion protocols, particularly chromic acid (CRA) versus inverse aqua regia (IAR), produce systematic offsets in reported Os isotopic compositions and concentrations from the same sediment samples. These discrepancies arise from the differential dissolution of mineral phases resultant from the variable acids used in such studies. Here, we compare Os isotopic compositions and concentrations from Pleistocene North Atlantic marine sediments digested with CRA and IAR, integrating X-ray diffraction and scanning electron microscopy coupled with electron backscatter diffraction of bulk sediments and post-digestion residues. Digestion via CRA consistently yields more radiogenic Os isotope ratios and lower concentrations than IAR. Analysis of post-digestion residues demonstrates that both methods primarily dissolve carbonates, while silicates and accessory minerals persist at varying degrees. These contrasting dissolution behaviors suggest CRA is more appropriate for sediments with low detrital input, while IAR can amplify detrital contributions. Our results highlight the critical need for standardized digestion protocols to ensure reproducible and comparable Os isotope chemostratigraphic records in both early Earth history and Quaternary sedimentary successions.

title: Trace element composition of cold-water corals from coastal antarctic surface sediments: Implications for biomineralization mechanisms and paleoceanographic reconstructions
description: Publication date: Available online 25 May 2026 Source: Chemical Geology Author(s): Derong Zhao, Sang Chen, Junru Guan, Haihong Wu, Xin Chen, Cong Zeng, Zhekai Tang, Maojun Yan, Ning Zhao, Liqiang Xu, Meng Zhou
abstract: The Southern Ocean is one of the most sensitive regions to ongoing climate change, and plays an important role in the global ocean circulation and carbon cycle through a range of physical, chemical and biological processes. Understanding long-term environmental changes in the Southern Ocean can help us better resolve the key processes influencing its impact on global climate. Paleoceanographic reconstructions in the Southern Ocean, however, are often challenging due to a lack of feasible archives and well-calibrated environmental proxies. Cold-water corals are a type of benthic organism of relatively high abundance in the Southern Ocean, with their calcium carbonate skeletons that can potentially record environmental changes at relatively high temporal resolution. Here we report measurements of the trace element composition of cold-water corals and a tubeworm collected from surface sediments in the Ross Sea and west of the Amundsen Sea. We find that spatial distribution of calcitic and aragonitic corals in the Southern Ocean is likely controlled by the bottom water carbonate saturation state. Trace element composition of the biogenic carbonates is mainly determined by their respective mineralogy and displays significant vital effects. Different element-to‑calcium ratios show strong correlations in individual organisms that are similar to cold-water corals found in other regions, and can generally be explained with existing biomineralization models. Several elemental ratio proxies show relations with environmental conditions that are consistent with global calibrations, most notably the Li/Mg-temperature relation in both biogenic aragonite and high-Mg calcite, yet large uncertainties remain in terms of their use in paleoceanographic reconstructions. Understanding the biomineralization mechanisms underlying the vital effects in different types of cold-water corals with in-situ analytical techniques and numerical models is a key step in improving the proxies that are suitable for the extreme environmental conditions in the Southern Ocean.

title: Geochemical and hydrological controls on aragonite versus calcite precipitation in speleothems and paleoclimatic implications
description: Publication date: Available online 25 May 2026 Source: Chemical Geology Author(s): Rui Zhang, Haiwei Zhang, Christoph Spötl, Carlos Pérez-Mejías, Zixin Guan, Heather Stoll, Yanjun Cai, Liangcheng Tan, Fudong Wang, Xunlin Yang, Yan Yang, Lijuan Sha, Jian Wang, Yina Song, Pengzhen Duan, Youfeng Ning, Hai Cheng
abstract: Speleothem mineralogy (aragonite vs. calcite) and geochemical signatures are governed by complex hydrological and geochemical processes. However, previous studies have predominantly focused on geochemical constraints, whereas the role of cave hydrological processes in regulating carbonate polymorphism has received far less attention. Furthermore, long-term in situ monitoring of the environmental conditions controlling aragonite and calcite precipitation in natural cave settings remains limited. Here, we combine three years of cave monitoring in Shennong Cave, southeastern China, with glass-plate observations and a global dripwater compilation to show that carbonate polymorphism is governed by threshold effects in Mg/Ca–calcite saturation index (SIcc) space, and that precipitation-driven prior carbonate precipitation (PCarbP) favors aragonite precipitation by increasing Mg/Ca while maintaining relatively low SIcc. At Mg/Ca values ≥ 1000 mmol/mol, Mg/Ca defines the threshold for aragonite occurrence and crystal elongation, whereas pH and SIcc are most closely associated with depositional proportion and crystal habit, respectively, with aragonite evolving from slender needles to shorter, thicker bundles as supersaturation increases. At aragonite-precipitating sites, PCarbP during wetter periods drives spatial partitioning of carbonate polymorphs on glass plates, with calcite precipitating at the drip-impact point and aragonite toward the margins, providing direct modern-process evidence for calcite–aragonite fabrics in speleothems. Monitoring results further show that aragonite- and calcite-precipitating sites differ in their hydrological setting, the extent of PCarbP, and the magnitude of Mg/Ca fluctuations. At the seasonal scale, reduced effective infiltration and intensified in-cave degassing drive substantial Mg/Ca increases at aragonite-precipitating sites, whereas lower soil and epikarst pCO2 primarily enhances PCarbP at calcite-precipitating sites. At the interannual scale, dripwater Mg/Ca declined from approximately 2000 to 500 mmol/mol from 2022 and 2025, broadly tracking the long-term increase in regional precipitation. Overall, this study demonstrates how cave hydrology and PCarbP control carbonate polymorphism in cave systems, and indicates that dripwater Mg/Ca reflects different hydroclimatic controls across seasonal and interannual timescales, improving the interpretation of speleothem mineralogy and geochemical proxies in paleoclimate studies.

title: Climate-driven hydrological shifts generate nutrient-mobilization hotspots in northern catchments: Evidence from the Vantaanjoki, Finland
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 676 Author(s): Abubaker Omer, Joy Bhattacharjee, Kati Anttila, Eliisa Lotsari, Harri Koivusalo
abstract: Evidence is accumulating that climate change is driving fundamental shifts in hydrological regimes across northern catchments. Yet the biogeochemical consequences of these shifts and their implications for surface-water quality remain poorly understood. Here, we developed a process-based diagnostic framework that integrates hydrology–water-quality modeling, climate scenarios (SSP1-2.6, SSP2-4.5, SSP5-8.5), and statistical methods to identify the mechanisms by which climate forcing generates new hotspots of nitrogen and phosphorus mobilization in northern catchments. The framework was applied to the Vantaanjoki catchment, a well-characterized northern system with a documented history ofnutrient export to the Gulf of Finland and the Baltic Sea. We found statistically significant hydrological shifts under climate change scenarios, characterized by reduced snow storage and intensified winter–autumn runoff. Phenological mismatch between nutrient supply and plant uptake is projected to intensify under climate change, with nutrient release and mobilization increasingly occurring during periods of low biological demand. Combined with hydrological shifts, this leads to higher off-season losses and a transition in nutrient inputs to the Gulf of Finland from melt- to rainfall-driven pathways. Consequently, the seasonal share of annual nutrient export is projected to decrease in spring from 33% to 23–28%, while increasing in winter and autumn from 24% to 27–31% and from 30% to 36–40%, respectively, under SSP scenarios relative to the current condition. Moreover, climate change is projected to alter the emergence and expansion of nutrient-mobilization hotspots in vulnerable cropland and urban–agricultural transition zones through hydrological shifts and weakened nutrient–biological coupling. Based on the study’s findings, we present a transferable, mechanism-guided nutrient management framework to address climate-driven biogeochemical risks in comparable systems worldwide.

title: A two-layer safe reinforcement learning framework for multi-constraint reservoir operation: Integrating action masking and lagrangian dual method
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 676 Author(s): Zaichao Xie, Xiaoli Zhang, Wei Xu, Guoguo Lin, Dong Li, Shuncai Zhang, Hongyan Chen, Sheng Yang
abstract: Reservoir operation is a safety-critical sequential decision problem that must balance multiple operational objectives under strict water-level and release constraints. However, Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) algorithms frequently violate safety constraints during exploration, limiting their applicability in real-world engineering. This study proposes a two-layer Safe Reinforcement Learning (SafeRL) framework. The first layer is a state-driven action mask that filters infeasible actions before policy sampling; the second layer is a Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO)-Lagrangian implementation that adaptively adjusts the constraint multiplier to balance safety and performance. Unlike single-mechanism approaches that rely solely on post-hoc correction or fixed penalties, this design combines proactive filtering with adaptive optimization. Additionally, a non-linear action mapping is introduced to improve learning efficiency in constraint-critical regions. The framework is validated on the Three Gorges Reservoir using 60 years (1965–2024) of daily inflow records. Results show that the Lagrangian dual method reduces the total absolute constraint cost by 71.5% and increases generation reward by 4.9% compared with the correction-based baseline. In the baseline evaluation, the FullMask reduces the action-correction violation rate from 21–79% to zero, and the square mapping yields a further 0.54% gain in total energy generation. These results support the proposed SafeRL framework as a model-consistent decision-support approach for long-horizon reservoir operation under the modeled constraints.

title: Large-scale evaluation of long-term water conservation capacity dynamics using satellite images
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 676 Author(s): Lei Wang, Yi Yi, Changsen Zhao, Zhongkun Luo, Chunhua He, Yanqing Lian, Guoqing Wang
abstract: Assessing water conservation functions is critical for sustainable water resource utilization under the changing climate. Spatiotemporal variations of water conservation capacity, driven by climate change and human activities, cause regional socio-economic disparities, yet existing methods fail to accurately characterize factor interactions and are limited to single underlying surfaces, reducing global applicability. To address this, this study integrates the Water Conservation Index (WCI) and geographic detector to evaluate 1985–2022 long-term dynamic changes of water conservation capacity and its driving factors in China’s Yellow River Water Conservation Area with complex underlying surface and severe climate change, improving large-scale research reliability. Results show an abrupt 2000 shift in capacity, decline then rise, consistent with climate change; it displays a south-high-north-low pattern, consistent with soil water content (SWC). SWC dominates spatial distribution, followed by EvapoTranspiration (ET), Land Surface Temperature (LST), and Leaf Area Index (LAI) yet precipitation drives SWC. Two-factor interactions between SWC and ET exceed single-factor effects. Post-2000, land use change, urban expansion, and GDP growth boosted Fractional Vegetation Cover (FVC) and thereafter capacity. These findings provide a theoretical and methodological foundation for water conservation protection under complex conditions, and scientific support for water resource allocation and climate change adaptation policies, facilitating global sustainable development.

title: Divergent effects of natural and socioeconomic drivers on water use in China from 2000 to 2022
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 676 Author(s): Tianqing Zhao, Wen Wang, Xueke Yan, Fuxiong Guo
abstract: The uneven distribution and imbalance between supply and demand of water resources in China pose serious challenges to sustainable socioeconomic development. This study examined the spatiotemporal dynamics of total water use (WU at the national scale, area-normalized as WU/A at the provincial scale), per capita water use (WU/C), and water use per 10,000 yuan of GDP (WU/G) at both the national and provincial scales from 2000 to 2022. A random forest regression model combined with the SHAP framework was applied to assess relative importance and contributions of natural factors (annual precipitation, annual mean temperature, and NDVI) and socioeconomic factors (cropland proportion, built-up land proportion, secondary industry proportion, population density, and GDP per capita) for each water use indicator. The results show that, at the national scale, population density, built-up land proportion, and NDVI are the dominant drivers of WU, WU/C, and WU/G. Economic factors dominate water use in most provinces, with built-up land proportion and population density exerting a negative impact on WU/G, whereas their effects on WU/A and WU/C vary regionally. For WU/C, provinces driven by both natural and socio-economic factors have a wider distribution. In contrast, WU/G is not dominated by natural factors in any province. These findings improve understanding of how natural and socioeconomic drivers affect water use patterns and provide a scientific basis for developing region-specific strategies for improving water-use efficiency.

title: Prediction of solute transport in three-dimensional rough-walled rock fractures: The role of geometrical heterogeneities
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 676 Author(s): Na Huang, Zhenhui Wang, Yujing Jiang, Ju Wang, Bo Li
abstract: Predicting solute transport in rough-walled rock fractures remains challenging due to geometric complexities. This study develops a direct predictive framework for solute transport in rock fractures by explicitly incorporating geometric heterogeneities characterized by relative standard deviation (RSD) of the local mechanical aperture and the contact area ratio (c r), under laminar flow conditions. We conducted a series of experimentally validated numerical simulations of solute transport in 3D rough-walled fractures with different apertures and contact areas. The resulting breakthrough curves (BTCs) were inversely analyzed by the classical advection dispersion equation (ADE). The fitted transport coefficients (transport velocity and hydrodynamic dispersion coefficient) were normalized against the smooth parallel-plate model, and subsequently parameterized in terms of RSD and c r. A semi-empirical analytical model is proposed that integrates these parameterized relationships into a modified ADE framework. The model enables direct prediction of solute transport based on measurable geometric parameters, without the need to resolve the velocity and concentration fields. It adaptively degenerates to the classical analytical solution for a smooth parallel-plate model when the geometric heterogeneity diminishes. Validation against fracture samples from prior experiments shows that the proposed model achieves high accuracy.

title: Enhancing simulation accuracy of a semi-distributed conceptual hydrological model using satellite soil moisture products
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 676 Author(s): Haotian Cai, Yi Nan, Rui Tong, Fuqiang Tian, Jingan Lin
abstract: An accurate representation of the soil moisture (SM) state is fundamental to both refining the physical basis of parameters and to reducing uncertainty of runoff simulation in conceptual hydrological models. However, the specific impacts and underlying mechanisms of incorporating passive satellite SM products into semi-distributed conceptual models remain unclear. To address this gap, we employed the semi-distributed conceptual hydrological model, Tsinghua Representative Elementary Watershed (THREW), in 12 diverse watersheds across China. We assimilated two multi-resolution (1 km and 36 km) SM products derived from the AMSR-E/2 series using an exponential filter. We designed and compared three calibration strategies: a runoff-only benchmark, and two joint scenarios using different SM product resolutions. Results demonstrate that the SM product reduces the overestimation of small-to-medium flood peaks by correcting the antecedent top-layer moisture of the model. This corrective effect is most pronounced during seasonal transitions of spring-to-summer and summer-to-autumn characterized by distinct wet-dry shifts of SM within the whole year mainly in humid subtropical monsoon climate regions. However, the simulation accuracy for large flood events was compromised when calibrating with satellite SM, primarily due to the inconsistent sensitivity to rainfall inputs between the satellite data and the modeled top-layer moisture. This limitation is effectively mitigated by replacing the stringent KGE metric evaluating SM simulation with weaker constraints: the correlation coefficient (R) and the ratio of standard deviations (SDR).

title: Occurrence and driving factors of microplastics in the surface water of a grassland river in China
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 676 Author(s): Tong Lin, Zeyuan Liu, Qifeng Liu, Ruihong Yu, Haizhu Hu
abstract: Microplastics (MPs) pollution in rivers has become a global environmental problem, especially in urban areas. The occurrence, drivers and risks of riverine MPs in rural areas remains poorly understood. This study investigated the spatiotemporal distribution, driving factors and ecological risk of MPs in a typical grassland river, Xilin River. Results showed that MPs abundance was significantly higher in the wet and dry seasons compared to the spring flood season. MPs abundance increased from the upper to the lower reaches. The dominant polymer types in the dry and wet seasons were polyethylene terephthalate (PET) and polyamide (PA). In the spring flood season, the proportion of PET decreased significantly, with a concurrent increase in Polyethylene (PE) and acrylate (ACR). Most MPs were pellets with size in 20–50 μm range. The Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling analysis showed that driving mechanisms of MPs abundance varied seasonally. The primary controls on MPs shifted from hydrodynamic conditions in the wet season to river water chemistry in the dry season, with a combination of hydrodynamic conditions and potential sources jointly controlling in the spring flood season. The spatial distribution of riverine MPs was shaped by hydrological forces in the upper reaches versus anthropogenic pressures in the lower reaches. The MPs pollution risk was highest in the densely populated lower reaches and lowest in the upper reaches. MPs risk levels were highest during the wet season and lowest during the spring flood season. This study provides a foundation for understanding and addressing MPs pollution in grassland river ecosystems.

title: Driving pathways and spatial heterogeneity of dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC) and organic carbon (DOC) in the Lijiang River Basin
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 676 Author(s): Yan Zhen, Xin Liu, Haodong Zheng, Qiong Xiao, Xiang Zeng, Xiaowei Liu, Yantao Deng
abstract: Karst riverine carbon export is jointly regulated by climate, topography, and ecological degradation/restoration. Clarifying the dominant controls on dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC) and dissolved organic carbon (DOC) across different section types, together with their underlying pathways, is essential for diagnosing watershed carbon processes and evaluating ecological restoration outcomes. Taking the Lijiang River Basin as a case study, this study integrates XGBoost–SHAP analysis with multi-group structural equation modeling (SEM) to disentangle the driver assemblages, directional responses, and direct–indirect effect chains governing DIC and DOC in three spatial groups of sampling sections: main-channel control sections, confluence-affected sections, and tributary sections. The results show that both DIC and DOC differ significantly among section types. XGBoost–SHAP analysis indicates that the key controls on DIC are primarily characterized by the joint constraint of topographic background and carbonate-weathering-derived solute signals, whereas the explanatory factors for DOC are relatively consistent across section types, being mainly regulated by external inputs and redox conditions. Multi-group SEM further reveals that DIC is produced predominantly through carbonate weathering. The influence of rocky desertification on DIC is exerted mainly indirectly, through alterations in carbonate weathering intensity and watershed solute supply, thereby generating section-dependent differences: its overall effect is suppressive in the main-channel and confluence-affected sections, but it can be promotive in tributary sections. DOC, by contrast, is chiefly controlled by the combined enhancement of allochthonous organic/solute inputs and intensified oxygen-consuming decomposition, and the direction of rocky desertification effects on DOC also varies among section types. These findings reveal the differential control mechanisms and spatial heterogeneity of DIC and DOC in karst watersheds, and provide a quantitative basis for section-specific carbon-process diagnosis and carbon export assessment under ecological management and restoration.

title: When heat meets drought: understanding the rising persistence of compound dry-hot extremes through Markov-Chain analysis
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 676 Author(s): Vikash Peepliwal, Somil Swarnkar, Abhinav Wadhwa, Radheshyam Sharma, Ashish Sharma
abstract: Understanding the dynamics of compound dry-hot extremes (CDHEs) is critical for climate risk assessment in semi-arid regions. This study over the state of Rajasthan in India investigates the evolution of rainfall deficits (defined by the 30th percentile precipitation threshold, P30) and temperature extremes (defined by the 70th percentile temperature threshold, T70), and their co-occurrence over six decades (1960–2024) using regridded district-level TerraClimate reanalysis data. Extreme thresholds were identified through percentile-based indices, and both frequency and persistence of events were analyzed. A first-order Markov chain framework developed based on exiting methodology was further applied to estimate stationary and transition probabilities, providing insights into long-term likelihoods and state-to-state shifts of compound extremes. Results show a fundamental spatio-temporal shift in extremes. Long-duration rainfall deficits that previously dominated the eastern and south-eastern regions have declined and are replaced by shorter but more frequent P30 events. Simultaneously, T70 events have increased sharply in frequency and persistence across the state, leading to more common co-occurrence of CDHE conditions. The early 2000s marked a peak in CDHE frequency and mean duration, particularly across central, south-western, and south-eastern Rajasthan. Stationary probabilities confirm that rainfall-only droughts since the 2000s occur infrequently, while heat-only and compound CDHE states persisted for all study period (1960–2024). Transition probabilities further indicate that both rainfall deficits and heat extremes have a high likelihood of evolving into compound states, with strong persistence once compounding begins. These findings highlight that Rajasthan’s climate is moving into a regime defined by frequent and intensified compound extremes. The shift poses adverse implications on agriculture, water resources, and livelihoods, underscoring the urgent need for designing integrated monitoring and adaptation strategies for similar semi-arid regions across the globe to address concurrent rainfall variability and rising temperatures.

title: Multi-scale reactive transport modeling of water–rock interactions during uranium in situ recovery
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 676 Author(s): Haohao Luo, Adam J. Siade, Chao Li, Baheten Boassen Guillaume Herman, Henning Prommer, Jing Sun
abstract: In situ recovery (ISR) is widely used for uranium mining without physical excavation of the ore. Successful ISR requires an accurate understanding of how lixiviants interact hydrochemically with the ore and how these processes scale from laboratory experiments to the field. Here, we developed a multi-scale reactive transport modeling (RTM) and uncertainty quantification framework to investigate water–rock interactions controlling uranium recovery during ISR under uncertainty. A laboratory-scale RTM was first constructed to analyze column leaching experiments on sandstone-hosted ores using acidic and alkaline lixiviants, and a particle swarm optimization-based Monte Carlo approach was used to quantify parameter uncertainty. The results show that uranium-bearing mineral dissolution was kinetically controlled, whereas gangue mineral dissolution competed for the lixiviant and delayed significant uranium leaching by approximately 72 h. The most sensitive and uncertain parameters were both associated with uranium dissolution kinetics. The model was subsequently extended to the field scale using residence time-dependent rate laws, incorporating a dual-domain transport framework and stochastic spatial heterogeneity. By propagating posterior geochemical parameter distributions from the laboratory-scale model, field-scale predictive uncertainty was assessed. The results indicate that physical heterogeneity and mass transfer limitations strongly shape the uncertainty distribution and prevent the over-optimistic recovery predicted by idealized homogeneous models. The predicted cumulative uranium recovery ranged from 1,139 to 1,630 kg, with a mean of 1,380 kg, and followed an approximately normal distribution. Uranium yields were governed by nonlinear multivariate interactions, with high recovery occurring when high initial uranium loading, fast dissolution kinetics, and low gangue interference coincided. This study constrains the water–rock interactions governing ISR and provides a process-based multi-scale modeling tool for prediction under uncertainty.

title: Modelling the spatial mismatch of nutrient sources and exports: A case study of Baiyangdian Basin, North China
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 676 Author(s): Yali Zhang, Qiangang Feng, Chunxue Yu, Zhihao Xu
abstract: Understanding how the spatial configuration of nutrient sources and exports regulates watershed nutrient delivery is critical for effective water quality management. However, nutrient load-based analyses often lack explicit metrics to quantify source-export mismatch, and thereby hindering targeted prioritization of interventions. We applied the SPAtially Referenced Regression On Watershed attributes (SPARROW) model over 2000–2020 to simulate nutrient generation, routing, and delivery in Baiyangdian Basin, China. The calibrated model explained 88% and 75% of spatial variability in total nitrogen (TN) and total phosphorus (TP) loads, respectively. Prior to 2015, TN and TP loads fluctuated around 400 t·yr−1 and 58 t·yr−1, respectively. Then the Ten-Point Water Plan implemented post-2015 reduced TN and TP loads by 43% and 38%, leading to decreases in in-lake nutrients concentration from 6 mg·L−1 to 3 mg·L−1 for TN and from 0.45 mg·L−1 to 0.30 mg·L−1 for TP. On average, point sources (PS) contributed nearly 70% of TN, but made comparable contributions to TP as non-point sources (NPS). Over time, the contribution of NPS increased from 28% to 40% for TN and from 52% to 61% for TP. We introduced a spatial mismatch index to quantify source-export divergences, revealing that 37.35% of sub-basins exhibited mismatches. High-input/low-export mismatches are concentrated in the central and southern plains where dense drainage ditches and sluggish flows enhance long-term average nutrient retention effect. Conversely, low-input/high-export mismatches prevail in the northern mountainous regions dominated by runoff-driven export. Temporal mismatches tracked the PS-NPS shift, with low-input/high-export areas expanding in response to increasing NPS loads. Our findings provide empirical evidence to guide differentiated watershed nutrient governance prioritization.

title: A study on a seepage detection method for Concrete Face Rockfill Dams coupling data-driven screening with multiphysics-field validation
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 676 Author(s): Caiyi Zhang, Jie Ren, Ying Li, Shenghao Nan
abstract: Seepage in Concrete Face Rockfill Dams is typically characterized by strong concealment and discretely distributed flow paths, making it difficult for a single monitoring or detection technique to effectively constrain leakage locations under complex engineering conditions. Therefore, this study proposes a leakage detection method for CFRDs that couples data-driven screening with multiphysics-field validation. First, monitoring data from piezometers and three-dimensional joint meters installed in the dam body are selected, and their statistical features are extracted as inputs. A Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise (DBSCAN) clustering method is then employed to identify anomalous monitoring points, enabling preliminary screening of potential leakage risk zones. Subsequently, the pseudo-flow field method is introduced to analyze the spatial distribution characteristics of electric potential differences, providing further spatial constraints on the screened zones and narrowing the range of potential leakage pathways. Building on this, ink injection experiments are conducted using an underwater robot to perform near-field observations in suspected leakage areas. Image enhancement algorithms are further applied to improve the distinguishability of ink trajectories, assisting in the identification of flow directions of weak leakage and their potential exit locations. Taking the upper reservoir of the WD pumped-storage power station as an engineering case, the results show that the spatial distribution of anomalous monitoring points, high electric potential difference zones identified by the pseudo-flow field analysis, and flow directions revealed by the underwater ink injection experiments exhibit good spatial consistency, allowing the leakage area to be progressively narrowed and located under engineering conditions. The study demonstrates that the proposed method can provide effective technical support for the rapid identification and engineering remediation of leakage hazards in CFRDs.

title: Tracing hydrological connectivity in a coastal salt marsh during intertidal exposure using stable isotopes
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 676 Author(s): Yue Liu, Zibo Yu, Junhong Bai, Weixiang Ren, Jichen Qiu, Yongkang Zhao
abstract: Hydrological connectivity is considered a key mechanism that governs wetland ecosystem functions. However, accurately quantifying hydrological connectivity during intertidal flat exposure periods remains a significant methodological challenge. Here, we developed a stable isotope-based hydrological connectivity index (HCIH and HCIO ) using stable water isotopes (δ2H and δ18O) as tracers. This method simplifies the complexity associated with the conventional hydrological connectivity index (HCI) established based on multiparameter datasets and provides a more precise quantification of hydrological connectivity during the tidal flat exposure phase. The results revealed significant spatial heterogeneity and seasonal variability in both HCIH and HCIO in low-, middle- and high- marsh zones (p 0.6) than HCIO , suggesting that HCIH may serve as a more reliable index for hydrological connectivity in the study area. Water source partitioning revealed that precipitation and seawater were the dominant sources in the middle- and low-marsh zones, whereas the high-marsh zones featured four water sources, including precipitation, seawater, groundwater, and river water. IsoSource analysis effectively resolved source ambiguity and improved the accuracy of the HCI (R2 > 0.7). These findings suggest a practical and accurate tool for quantifying hydrological connectivity dynamics during tidal flat exposure, contributing to the optimization of tidal creek networks in coastal wetland hydrological restoration practices.

title: Groundwater-mediated controls and future projections of carbon stocks in coastal wetlands
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 676 Author(s): Xulong Gong, Ying Liang, Xue Jiang, Rui Ma, Yuan Liu, Shun Hu, Yanxin Wang
abstract: Coastal wetlands are critical blue carbon reservoirs, yet the role of groundwater dynamics in regulating carbon stocks remains poorly quantified in current assessments. Taking the Jiangsu coastal wetland area as the study site, this study quantified the spatial distribution of carbon stocks, identified key environmental drivers, and projected future carbon stock trajectories under sea-level rise scenarios. An integrated framework combining linear mixed effects models, structural equation modeling, ensemble machine learning models, and land-use simulation was developed to assess carbon stocks from 1988 to 2022 and project their changes to 2100. The results showed that climatic factors uniquely contributed more than 30% to aboveground biomass, whereas groundwater hydrodynamic and hydrochemical variables jointly accounted for a unique contribution of 14.2% to the variation in soil organic carbon. Structural equation modeling suggested that groundwater-mediated pathways were more strongly associated with climate-driven variation in soil organic carbon density than vegetation-mediated pathways. Historical analysis indicated that total carbon stocks declined by 35.1% from 1988 to 2022, mainly associated with land-use conversion and sea-level rise. To forecast future changes, a novel dual scale projection framework was developed to simultaneously account for shifts in carbon density and wetland spatial extent. Compared with the 4 mm/y sea-level-rise scenario, the 7 mm/y scenario produced a net carbon stock loss of 3.7 × 103 t by 2100. This study advances the understanding of groundwater-mediated controls on coastal carbon stocks and provides a transferable modeling framework for blue carbon management under climate change.

title: Unveiling urban process-dependent hydrological responses via rainfall “fingerprints”
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 676 Author(s): Ting Liu, Lina Yuan, Yuying Li, Zijiang Song, Linlin Ye, Ao Xu, Tsering Namgyal, Chao Li, Min Liu
abstract: Characterizing rainfall variability is essential for hydrometeorological analysis and building flood-resilient cities. However, progress is hindered by an incomplete grasp of rainfall heterogeneity, ambiguous links to hydrological impacts, and a lack of tools for systematically and operationally identifying event-scale rainfall processes. Here, we analyze 23 years of hourly rainfall observations from 61 gauges in Shanghai and introduce an integrated machine learning methodology combining unsupervised and supervised learning to: (1) extract reproducible spatiotemporal rainfall “fingerprints,” hydrologically meaningful event-scale rainfall process archetypes, (2) validate their hydrological responses, and (3) build an automated fingerprint classifier. A pronounced west–east contrast in fingerprint diversity emerges across the city, with more homogenized fingerprints in highly urbanized sectors. Fingerprints also display strong spatiotemporal heterogeneity in rainfall process evolution, forming station-specific archetypes that are internally coherent yet indistinguishable by rainfall intensity or accumulation alone. Hydrological analysis reveals an asymmetric relationship between rainfall fingerprints and hydrological response: peak water level is primarily associated with cumulative rainfall and duration, whereas the rising rate is more sensitive to peak intensity. Identical fingerprints can produce different responses, while distinct fingerprints may yield similar responses under varying boundary conditions. The proposed classifier achieves > 80% accuracy in identifying the rainfall fingerprints of unseen events at over 50 stations, supporting the potential for automated rainfall process type recognition. The methodology established here not only deepens understanding of urban rainfall but also provides a scientific and technical foundation for site-adaptive, process-informed urban flood governance.

title: Unravelling global patterns of drought-flood alternations
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 676 Author(s): Gebremedhin Gebremeskel Haile, Md Sariful Islam, Qiuhong Tang, Danielle Wood
abstract: Droughts and floods are among the most damaging climate extremes, yet their abrupt alternations, rapid shifts from one to the other, remain poorly understood on a global scale. This study presents a comprehensive spatiotemporal analysis of abrupt drought-to-flood (DTF) and flood-to-drought (FTD) alternations worldwide from 1981 to 2023. Results show that these events are frequent, spatially widespread, and often occur concurrently with increasing levels of abrupt transitions in both directions. Regions with increasing FTD and DTF trends include the Yangtze Basin, Eastern India, Pakistan, and Southeast Africa, while California, Southern Africa, and Emilia-Romagna show declining trends, with California exhibiting a statistically significant decrease in FTD events (p < 0.1). In Southern Africa, the FTD coverage peaked at 5.5% in 1990, then declined to 4.6% in 2016. Emilia-Romagna (Italy) demonstrated greater temporal variability, with FTD areas rising from 7% in 1982 to 11% in 2005, before falling to 9% by 2022. DTF events were most frequent in Southern Africa (7.06 DTFs in 43 years) and Emilia-Romagna (7.13), while FTD events were highest in the Mississippi (8.73) and Yangtze (6.86) basins. Conversely, Eastern India and California exhibited consistently low frequencies of both DTF and FTD. These spatial disparities underscore the complex and region-specific dynamics of hydroclimatic extremes. Improved understanding of drought-flood alternations is essential for strengthening early warning systems, risk management, and adaptation strategies in vulnerable regions worldwide.

title: Enhancing large-scale streamflow prediction by coupling structural inductive bias with meta-learning
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 675 Author(s): Xuan Tang, Yuting Zhao, Yuan Yu, MingRui Yu, Guanghua Qin, Hongxia Li
abstract: Deep learning has opened new opportunities for streamflow modeling, enabling the extraction of complex hydrological patterns from large-sample observations. However, large-scale streamflow prediction remains challenging, requiring robust generalization across diverse hydroclimatic conditions and reliable transfer to ungauged regions. To address these challenges, we propose a MAML-EA-LSTM framework that integrates Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML) with an entity-aware Long Short-Term Memory (EA-LSTM) architecture. The framework is evaluated using 468 basins from the CAMELS dataset. Results show that the proposed MAML-EA-LSTM achieves a mean Nash-Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE) of 0.75, outperforming LSTM (0.70), EA-LSTM (0.69), MAML-LSTM (0.71), and the conceptual Sacramento Soil Moisture Accounting (SAC-SMA) model (0.57), with improvements observed in most basins. Reductions in both high-flow and low-flow bias further indicate enhanced predictive stability across contrasting hydrological conditions. Dominant attribute identification analysis shows that MAML-EA-LSTM also improves hydrological behavior learning, yielding an overall hit rate of 71.2%, higher than LSTM (43.6%), EA-LSTM (60.7%) and MAML-LSTM (51.5%). Transfer experiments under strictly spatially disjoint conditions further demonstrate stronger out-of-sample transferability in data-scarce basins. The proposed framework achieves an NSE of 0.553 with only one year of target-basin observations for fine-tuning. These findings indicate that the integration of structural inductive bias and meta-learning provides a promising pathway toward more robust and transferable large-sample hydrological modeling.

title: A physics-informed multi-scale fourier neural operator framework for snow avalanche dynamics simulation
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 675 Author(s): Xingkai Li, Yuanjun Jiang, Yu Zhuang, Xiaobo Hu, Binbin Zhao
abstract: Avalanches are typical natural disasters in alpine watersheds. Near-real-time early warning and multi-scenario risk assessment require a balance between physical consistency and computational efficiency, yet traditional numerical solvers often suffer from severe computational bottlenecks in high-resolution simulations or large-scale scenario ensemble computations. To address this issue, this study proposes a Physics-Informed Neural Operator (PINO) framework for the efficient prediction of avalanche dynamic processes. The framework uses the Fourier Neural Operator as the backbone network and incorporates residual constraints of governing equations. By introducing architectural enhancements including dimensionless physical loss, a spatial feature extractor, and a channel attention mechanism, the model’s ability to learn complex avalanche evolution processes under varying terrain and physical parameters is significantly improved. Meanwhile, an active-region-prioritized sampling scheme and a progressive training strategy further enhance training efficiency. The model is trained and evaluated solely on 12 heterogeneous multi-scenario datasets generated by the RAMMS software. Results demonstrate that the model achieves relatively stable accuracy under cross-parameter and cross-terrain conditions, and its performance is significantly superior to traditional Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs).Its zero-shot super-resolution performance also outperforms the standard FNO. Benchmark tests show that the inference time reaches the near-real-time level of seconds to tens of seconds, providing a feasible and novel paradigm for multi-scenario risk assessment and near-real-time prediction of avalanches and other shallow surface flow dynamic processes in alpine watersheds.

title: Machine learning models unravel contrasting enrichment of uranium and arsenic in groundwater from the Songnen Basin, China
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 675 Author(s): Haowei Sun, Zhipeng Gao, Wengeng Cao, Xiaosi Su, Huaming Guo
abstract: The differential enrichment of uranium (U) and arsenic (As) in groundwater poses significant threats to drinking water safety and complicates water resource management. Although the contrasting geochemical behaviors of U and As in groundwater have been generally recognized, the key factors controlling their spatial distribution along a hydrogeochemical profile remain poorly quantified. This study combined hydrogeochemical analysis with an interpretable machine learning model to identify the dominant processes governing the differential distribution of U and As in groundwater of the Songnen Basin, China. Along the groundwater flow path, U concentrations decreased (from 31.8 to 0.37 μg/L), in contrast to the increasing trend of As levels (from 0.83 to 338 μg/L). This contrasting behavior was predicted using three different models (support vector regression, random forest, and extreme gradient boosting), among which the random forest model achieved the best performance. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis furtheridentified NO3 – and Ca2+ as the most influential factors for U enrichment in oxic-suboxic zones, indicating that U was mainly mobilized by NO3 –-mediated U(IV) oxidation to U(VI), followed by the formation of highly soluble Ca-U-CO3 complexes. In contrast, the SHAP analysis revealed DOC, Fe(II), Mn2+, and HCO3 – as the key drivers of As mobilization in anoxic zones, suggesting that As release was primarily governed by the reductive dissolution of As-bearing Fe/Mn oxides mediated by dissolved organic matter degradation, along with competitive adsorption by HCO3 –. Anoxic conditions, characterized by negative ORP values and high Fe(II) and Mn2+ concentrations, facilitated the reduction of U(VI) to U(IV), thereby resulting in low dissolved U concentrations in the anoxic zones. This study provides a replicable framework for deciphering the contrasting behaviors of U and As in groundwater, thereby enabling the identification of safe drinking water sources with low concentrations of both U and As.

title: Nutrient cycling, biogeochemical pathways and eutrophication status of an urban Himalayan lake system
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 675 Author(s): Gh Jeelani, Suhail A. Lone, M. Saleem Dar, Javid A. Ganai, Niharika Sharma, Sanjeev Kumar
abstract: Urban freshwater lakes in high-altitude Himalaya are increasingly threatened by eutrophication due to accelerated nutrient loading from anthropogenic and climatic pressures. This study presents an integrated assessment of nutrient sources, transformation pathways, and eutrophication processes in Dal Lake, Western Himalaya, using a novel combination of seasonal profiling of nutrients (NO3 –, NH4 +, TP, TN, POM), stable isotope biogeochemistry (δ13C and δ15N), Self-Organizing Maps (SOM), hydrodynamic-nutrient transport modeling, and Bayesian source apportionment (MixSIAR). Seasonal monitoring of NO3 –, NH4 +, TN, TP and POM revealed significant spatio-temporal heterogeneity, with elevated nutrient concentration during winter and spring associated with reduced biological uptake and intensified internal loading. δ15N and δ13C values provided diagnostic signatures of nutrient processing, showing higher δ15N in summer-autumn due to microbial nitrification–denitrification and lower δ13C values during peak algal productivity. SOM clustering revealed distinct nutrient regimes shaped by external inputs (e.g., sewage, agricultural runoff) and internal biogeochemical processes (e.g., remineralization, microbial transformation). The MixSIAR model identified sewage (41.2%) and algal biomass (33.4%) as dominant contributors to POM in summer, with seasonal transition to agricultural and terrestrial sources. Hydrodynamic nutrient simulations indicated rapid NH4 + depletion, delayed NO3 – accumulation, and persistent TP concentration, emphasizing redox-sensitive nitrogen removal and sediment-driven phosphorus retention. Trophic state classification using Carlson’s Trophic State Index (TSI) placed most lake segments within eutrophic to hypereutrophic categories, corroborated by low Secchi disk depths and high TP levels, particularly near inflow and floating gardens. The results underscore a complex interplay of external nutrient inputs, internal biogeochemical cycling, and lake hydrodynamics in driving eutrophication. These insights provide a system-level understanding of nutrient fate in urban Himalayan lakes and support the development of targeted, climate-resilient restoration strategies.

title: Advancing drought monitoring with a three-dimensional feature space framework
description: Publication date: Available online 28 May 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology Author(s): Minghan Cheng, Zhangxin Liu, Jingwen Sun, Linyu Wang, Zhengxian Zhang, Xiuliang Jin, Chengming Sun
abstract: Accurate agricultural drought monitoring is fundamental to effective management strategies. Feature space methods have proven robust and are extensively utilized in this domain. To address lingering uncertainties—specifically the nonlinear characteristics of dry/wet limits, the influence of spatial domain size, and the scalability of three-dimensional feature spaces—this study developed and compared the land-air temperature difference (dT)-NDVI space and the LST-NDVI-NSAT space. Utilizing remotely sensed land surface temperature (LST), NDVI, and near-surface air temperature (NSAT), we evaluated the performance of the Temperature Vegetation Dryness Index (TVDI) and the Three-dimensional Drought Index (TDDI). The findings demonstrate that: (1) Nonlinear (quadratic) functions provide a superior fit for the dry/wet limits, with the three-dimensional configuration achieving higher precision; (2) The LST-NDVI-NSAT space stabilizes when the domain size encompasses a sufficient range of hydrothermal extremes, yielding highly consistent TDDI values; (3) TDDI exhibits a significant correlation with soil moisture content (SMC), which is further amplified under drought conditions. Compared to TVDI, VHI, and NDVI, TDDI more accurately delineates the temporal evolution of drought. Consequently, this study provides a reliable and transferable quantitative framework for drought monitoring and offers novel insights into feature space-based methodologies

title: Temporal inductive biases in hourly flood forecasting: a comparative analysis of recurrent, attention-based, and state-space neural networks
description: Publication date: Available online 28 May 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology Author(s): Binlan Zhang, Chaojun Ouyang, Qingsong Xu, Yanlin Liu, Zili Wang, Quan Tang
abstract: Daily-resolution flood forecasts often encounter difficulties in capturing rapid runoff fluctuations over short time periods. To address this limitation, moving to hourly-scale modeling is essential, yet identifying which deep learning architectures possess the optimal temporal inductive biases for such high-frequency dynamics remains an open challenge. In this study, we conduct a comprehensive comparative analysis of recurrent, attention-based, and state-space neural networks, benchmarked against simple layered structures on discharge-assisted forecasting tasks across 516 CAMELS catchments. The results indicate that the Patch Transformer achieves the best predictive performance. This suggests that patch-based processing acts as a superior inductive bias by smoothing high-frequency noise and extracting local temporal semantics, which effectively captures long-term routing and hydrological dependencies better than point-wise attention. While the traditional LSTM maintains robust performance, the Mamba model demonstrates a promising balance between accuracy and computational efficiency. Furthermore, through an interpretability analysis combining attention weights with Integrated Gradients (IG), we reveal that attention models successfully capture physical hydrological patterns, such as time-lagged responses and the dominance of dynamic meteorological drivers over static attributes. This work offers theoretical insights into how architectural choices determine short-term forecasting capability under diverse hydro-climatic regimes.

title: Applicability of an analytical probabilistic stormwater management model for large rural watersheds
description: Publication date: Available online 27 May 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology Author(s): Lauren McGregor, Sonia Hassini
abstract: Accurate peak flow predictions are critical for effective stormwater management. A wide range of techniques has been developed to estimate peak flows at pour points of interest. In many cases, the suitability of a model for a given watershed depends on numerous factors such as climate, catchment characteristics, data availability, and project objectives. This study focuses on extending the applicability of the Analytical Probabilistic Stormwater Management Model (APSWM), which was developed for small urban catchments. The APSWM peak flow model was recently enhanced to incorporate trapezoidal hydrograph shapes, referred to as APSWM(Tra), beyond the original triangular assumption. The model’s performance was investigated in a relatively large rural watershed within the Upper Thames River Basin in southwestern Ontario, Canada. APSWM(Tra) predicted peak flows within 14% of observed rates for return periods of 2, 5, 10, 25, 50, and 100 years and had a percent bias (PBIAS) of 13%. However, 2- and 5-year peak flows were underestimated. The study results suggest that APSWM(Tra) shows good potential as a tool for further development and use in large rural watersheds but further investigations and validations would be required before broader application.

title: Perspectives of co-extraction of geothermal heat with the critical raw materials lithium and copper from sedimentary basin fluids on the example of the North German Basin
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Geothermics, Volume 140 Author(s): Simona Regenspurg, Elisabeth Eiche, Katharina Alms, Ralph Bäßler, Guido Blöcher, Valentin Goldberg, Hannes Hofmann, Katrin Kieling, Christine Rösch, Lars Rüpke, Sylvia Sander, André Stechern, Katharina Sielemann, Philipp Weis
abstract: The co-extraction of critical raw materials (CRMs) and heat from geothermal fluids offers a promising approach to simultaneously address the increasing global demands for both, metals and energy. In brines from sedimentary basins, high concentrations of lithium and other CRMs such as copper, are emerging as an attractive complementary resource for mining, because these types of geological settings are ubiquitously occurring within the continental crust. In this contribution, we investigate the North German Basin as an example for an underexplored sedimentary reservoir, with lithium (and to a minor extend copper) serving as representative CRMs. We summarize the current state of knowledge and main perspectives that are relevant for co-extraction of CRMs and heat. We identified five key controlling factors: (1) the source and mobility of lithium in geothermal brines; (2) the feasibility of brine production from a low-permeability sandstone reservoir including exploitation, management, and sustainability of extraction by considering potential lithium co-production rates on the example of a well in the North German Basin; (3) thermal-hydraulic challenges in combined heat and lithium production; (4) suitable material selection to prevent severe corrosion and associated damages; and (5) environmental, social, governance aspects, as well as life cycle assessment of such co-production. In conclusion, the current data indicate that sedimentary basins fluids offer great potential for co-extraction of geothermal heat and critical raw materials (CRM) like Li and Cu, but at current state more demonstrators are needed to prove the technical and economic feasibility of CRM and heat co-extraction.

title: Prototype of a global model for regulating ecosystem services of inland wetlands
description: Publication date: 15 July 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1040 Author(s): Jeroen J.M. de Klein, Jan H. Janse, Anne A. van Dam, Edwin M.A. Hes, Rens van Beek, Isabel Wallnöfer, Jos T.A. Verhoeven
abstract: Natural wetlands deliver a range of ecosystem services like water, food and fibre provisioning, carbon sequestration, nutrient retention, and support for biodiversity. With respect to climate change, wetlands may act as a carbon sink or source, depending on management conditions. Despite their value, wetlands are disappearing at an alarming rate, and threatened by hydrological alteration, pollution and climate change. For an effective wetland policy there is a need to relate the state of wetlands to regional and global land-use and climate change projections, and to relate ecosystem services to wetland processes. Wetlands are, however, generally under-represented in global models and assessments. Here we present a model that estimates vegetation biomass production, carbon emissions, and water quality of freshwater wetlands on a global scale with different hydrological and climate conditions. The main hydro-ecological processes are described in a generic way, accounting for climate zones, water level fluctuations and main hydrological types: rain-/groundwater fed (ponded) wetlands and surface water-fed floodplain wetlands (flooded). The model is coupled to global hydrological (PCR-GLOBWB) and climate and land-use (IMAGE-GNM) models. It estimates the wetlands ecosystem services, in particular regulating ecosystem services like water availability, carbon sequestration/emission and nutrient retention that are difficult to quantify otherwise. The model was applied to several wetland types in widely varying climate regions (Sweden, Germany, Spain, subtropical China, tropical Brazil and Kenya). Results show that the model generates plausible results compared to measured data of greenhouse gas emissions and nutrient concentrations. Furthermore, the model can discriminate between wetlands with different environmental conditions, resulting in wetlands being either a sink or a source of carbon. A regionalized parameterization is in progress. Further potential applications of model outcomes include regional assessments of wetland ecosystem services, determining ecosystem services under alternative management, climate and land use scenarios, and link these to conditions for biodiversity.

title: Winter inversions and summer smoke: A season-dependent approach to PM₂.₅ modeling with low-cost sensors in complex terrain
description: Publication date: 15 July 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1040 Author(s): Alan Swanson, Ava Orr, Zachary A. Holden, Kyle Bocinsky, Erin L. Landguth
abstract: Accurate PM2.5 monitoring in complex terrain is challenged by sparse regulatory networks and distinct seasonal pollution sources, like winter temperature inversions and summer wildfires. This study develops and evaluates a hybrid modeling framework that integrates bias-corrected low-cost sensor data to improve spatial and temporal PM2.5 mapping in Montana, USA. We first applied a local, observation-based bias correction to dense PurpleAir sensor network, substantially improving agreement with reference monitors (R2 increased from 0.750 for a generic correction to 0.838). This corrected data was used to create high-resolution smog potential (smogP) surface, a static layer representing terrain-driven pollution accumulation, which explained 59.5% of the spatial variance of mean PM2.5 during wintertime inversion events. Daily 600 m resolution PM2.5 grids were then generated using geographically weighted regression framework. Cross-validation revealed a strong seasonal dichotomy in model performance: during the winter inversion season (November–March), models incorporating the smogP layer were critical and consistently outperformed other approaches. Conversely, during the summer wildfire season (May–September), the high density of sensor data alone was often sufficient, with simpler spatial interpolation models proving as effective at capturing the diffuse nature of large smoke plumes than models constrained by static covariates like smogP or satellite aerosol optical depth (AOD). We conclude that the optimal strategy for PM2.5 mapping in complex terrain is season-dependent, and this work provides a framework for leveraging citizen-science data to enhance air quality forecasting in these challenging environments. Synopsis Effective PM2.5 monitoring/modeling in complex terrain requires a seasonally adaptive strategy, using a terrain-based smog potential model for winter inversions and flexible spatial interpolation of dense sensor data for summer wildfire smoke.

title: Cord-blood black carbon burden is associated with coordinated inflammatory and heme-metabolic transcriptional programs at birth in Bradford, United Kingdom
description: Publication date: 15 July 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1040 Author(s): Houman Kahroba, Kenneth Vanbrabant, Marcel van Herwijnen, Rick Kamps, Dagmar Waiblinger, Matthew Walker, Marcel Ameloot, Maarten Roeffaers, John Wright, Tim Nawrot, Theo M. de Kok, Julian Krauskopf
abstract: Prenatal exposure to ambient air pollution has been linked to adverse perinatal and childhood outcomes, yet the molecular consequences of fetal black carbon (BC) exposure remain poorly characterized. In this prospective study nested within the Born in Bradford's Better Start cohort and the wider Born in Bradford data linkage cohort, we examined the association between cord-blood BC burden and neonatal cord-blood gene expression at birth. BC particles were quantified in cord blood using label-free femtosecond pulsed-laser microscopy, and transcriptomic profiling was performed with the BioSpyder TempO-Seq whole-transcriptome platform. Of 109 mother-infant pairs with exposure measurements and metadata, 83 samples passed transcriptomic quality control and were included in the analysis. Gene-level associations with log10-transformed BC were evaluated using limma-voom models adjusted for library batch, infant sex, cohort source, and maternal age. Pathway-level analyses were performed using CAMERA, with fry as sensitivity analysis, and robustness of pathway-contributing genes was assessed using 100 repeated 20% holdout analyses. No individual genes remained significant after false discovery rate correction across 9941 tested genes. In contrast, CAMERA identified two enriched Hallmark pathways associated with higher cord-blood BC: negative enrichment of heme metabolism and positive enrichment of TNFα signaling via NF-κB. These two pathways showed concordant directions in fry analysis, although they did not reach statistical significance in that framework. Additional Hallmark, GO Biological Process, and Reactome signals were directionally consistent but did not survive multiple-testing correction. Of 233 directional genes extracted from the two significant Hallmark pathways, 184 remained stable across repeated holdout analyses.
